cues.text: A Pope in Exile
By the 1240s, Pope Innocent IV found himself locked in the same kind of struggle with Emperor Frederick II that had convulsed his predecessors' relations with earlier emperors.
The struggle was sharper still, since Frederick controlled territory on nearly every side of the Papal States.
He had already seized church lands and captured a hundred prelates traveling to a Roman council in 1241.
Fearing for his safety in Italy, Innocent secretly fled Rome in 1244, traveled by sea, and arrived at the free city of Lyon , just outside imperial and French royal reach, in December of that year.
From this refuge, Innocent summoned bishops and princes across Christendom to a general council, which opened on June 28, 1245 .
It was the first ecumenical council held outside Rome's Lateran Basilica since the schism with the East, a striking sign of how precarious the pope's own position in Italy had become.
The Five Wounds of the Church
Innocent opened the council with a memorable sermon describing what he called the Church's five sorrows: the poor conduct of clergy and faithful, and the advance of the Saracens.

These included the ongoing schism with the Greeks, the devastation the Mongols (Tatars) had recently inflicted on Hungary, and — placed last but foremost in his mind — the persecution of the Church by Emperor Frederick II.
Frederick, summoned to answer charges of heresy, sacrilege, and breach of faith, did not appear in person, sending his envoy Thaddeus of Suessa to plead for delay.
The pope granted successive postponements, but when Frederick still failed to appear by the third session on July 17, Innocent proceeded to judgment.
The Deposition of an Emperor
On July 17, 1245, Innocent IV formally pronounced Frederick II deposed from the imperial throne and the Kingdom of Sicily, releasing his subjects from their oaths of loyalty.
The sentence was signed by some 150 bishops present and entrusted to the Dominican and Franciscan orders for publication throughout Europe.
The deposition proved far easier to declare than to enforce.
The pope lacked any army capable of making the sentence effective, and Frederick, though he lost ground steadily in the years that followed, continued to reign and fight until his death in 1250.
The conflict between pope and emperor that the council had hoped to settle instead continued, in modified form, for years afterward.
Other Business
Beyond its confrontation with Frederick, the council addressed pressing concerns across Christendom.
It voted funds and organized measures to defend Christian Europe against further Mongol incursions.
These followed the devastating invasions of Hungary and Poland, while the council took up appeals for aid to the beleaguered Latin Empire of Constantinople and the crusader states in the Holy Land.
The council also issued disciplinary constitutions on excessive use of excommunication and interdict, judicial procedure, and clerical dress.
It is credited with introducing the red hat as a mark of the cardinalate, a distinction still in use today.
Legacy
First Lyon strikingly illustrates how far the medieval struggle between papal and imperial authority could escalate.
A pope, driven from Italy, used a general council convened on foreign soil to strip an emperor of his throne.
Though the sentence against Frederick did not achieve its immediate political aim, it marked the definitive rupture between the last great Hohenstaufen emperor and the papacy.
This conflict would only be resolved by Frederick's death and the eventual extinction of his line within a generation.
The council also set an important precedent by relocating a general council away from Rome for reasons of papal safety, a pattern that would recur at the Second Council of Lyon three decades later.
